source.title: NeurIPS 2025 E2LM Competition : Early Training Evaluation of Language Models
source.authors: Mouadh Yagoubi; Yasser Dahou; Billel Mokeddem; Younes Belkada; Phúc H. Lê Khắc; Basma El Amel Boussaha; Réda Alami; Jingwei Zuo; Damiano Marsili; Mugariya Farooq; M. Lalmas; Georgia Gkioxari; Patrick Gallinari; P. Torr; Hakim Hacid

record.file_problem: Whole paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates downstream benchmark scores across model sizes and training progress, a different measure from the pretraining-loss scaling laws, and reports where those signals do and do not distinguish models.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan and Hoffmann and discusses validation loss, but does not fit loss power laws, test small-run extrapolation, or measure compute-optimal parameter/token allocations. It reports benchmark evaluations and validation-loss comparisons; no numerical validation-loss values are stated in the text, and Figure 8 is not transcribed numerically.
record.test_reason: The study does not fit scaling laws. Its benchmark curves for 0.5B, 1B and 3B models over 0–200B training tokens show whether downstream scores order by scale. That bears on V6 in a new setting: small models early in training. The result depends on the benchmark. Standard MMLU shows 'no apparent scaling law or pattern'; MMLU-var ranks models by size.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors add that MMLU shows no apparent scaling pattern early in training, while the cloze-format MMLU-var orders models by size. They also note that raw validation loss is a limited proxy for capability across data domains and in early training.
record.recipe_differences: This is a benchmark-design and early-training evaluation study, not a scaling-law fit or compute-allocation experiment; it uses benchmark scores and qualitative validation-loss comparisons rather than fitted held-out-loss power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Benchmark choice changes whether sizes and architecture variants are differentiated (MMLU versus MMLU-var); the data mixture changes MMLU-var results and validation-loss gaps across datasets.

fits_no_version.finding: MMLU-var favours the knowledge-mixture model, while HellaSwag shows similar scores for both mixtures.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How sensitive downstream benchmark scores are to the training-data mixture varies by benchmark.

fits_no_version.finding: Validation-loss gaps between the data mixtures are small in-domain and large out-of-domain. Early loss trajectories are similar for both.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Validation-loss comparisons depend on the evaluation dataset and training stage.

record.problems: The loss discussion is qualitative in the text and numerical values are only in a figure; the validation datasets other than FineWebEdu are not named in the discussion. Figure 3 has a model-size inconsistency: its caption says 0.5B, while the prose and appendix say 1B.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results on scaling-law fits, extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation were reported, so none were eligible as rows.

untested.parts: No loss power-law fit in parameters, tokens or compute.
Deep and wide variants differ in parameter count and are compared only on benchmarks. The authors state the width-versus-depth comparison is out of scope.
No other modalities or training regimes.

There is no quantitative fit of downstream score against scale or against pretraining loss. The loss-to-capability link is discussed only qualitatively (Appendix H). Nothing is reported beyond 3B or 200B tokens; 1T-token checkpoints are hidden.
No fitted exponents or fitting-choice comparisons.

missing.what: Many other benchmarks are plotted across sizes and tokens with no row. The text says GPQA, MATH, MuSR and MMLU-Pro are noisy and lack a clear signal. HellaSwag, WinoGrande, ARC-Easy and SciQ are said to give meaningful early signals.
missing.locator: Section 1.1 Figure 1; Section 1.4; Appendix A Figure 4; Appendix G

missing.what: Signal-quality monotonicity scores track how monotonically benchmark scores improve with training tokens. Overall SQ is 0.959 for MMLU-var, 0.285 for MMLU and 0.227 for GPQA. Per-model monotonicity for MMLU-var is 0.94–0.97.

record.verdict_notes: This is a competition proposal, not a scaling study. Its V6 bearing comes only from three model sizes and qualitative statements about figures. Kaplan and Hoffmann are cited but not tested. The 1B ranking consistency of 0.51 (Table 4) shows architecture ordering within a size is unstable even on MMLU-var.

versions.untested_parts: No power-law fit or test of held-out loss against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token fit.
Architecture variants are compared on benchmark scores, not at fixed parameter count using held-out loss.
No other-modality or alternative-training-regime power-law test.
The study evaluates benchmark behavior during training and across model sizes, but does not quantify downstream performance as a function of pretraining loss.

The study discusses differences in validation-loss ranges across datasets, but does not test dependence of fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits on fitting choices, nor fit curves for bends away from power laws.

rows.subject: 0.5B, 1B, and 3B models; six architecture configurations (aggregate result)
rows.stage_stated: pretraining checkpoints up to 200 billion tokens
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated standard MMLU across training checkpoints and model configurations.

conditions.value: two architecture variants at each of 0.5B, 1B, and 3B

rows.measure: Benchmark score differentiation across model sizes and architectures
rows.value: No consistent differentiation or apparent scaling pattern; around 180 billion tokens, 3B-Arch-2 clearly outperforms the others.
rows.note: Aggregate statement in the text; the paper does not provide numerical score values here.
rows.check: The authors say MMLU shows 'no apparent scaling law or pattern' across sizes. The only exception is 3B-Arch-2 near 180BT. That is absence of size ordering, not a partial effect. Values are figure-only.

rows.measure: Benchmark score ranking by model size and distinction between architecture variants
rows.value: The benchmark gives informative results throughout training, ranks models by size, and distinguishes architecture variants within a size.
rows.note: Aggregate statement in the text; the paper does not provide numerical score values here.
rows.check: This is a qualitative claim read from Figure 2 with no numbers in the text. Only three sizes are compared and no predictive fit is made. Ordering by size is observed; 'predictably' is not quantified.

relationships.reason: MMLU scores do not separate model sizes except 3B-Arch-2 late in training (R1). Figure 1 shows GPQA, MATH and MuSR are similarly noisy (text, not rowed). Size-ordered downstream gains fail here for small, early-trained models.
relationships.display_finding: MMLU separated sizes only for 3B-Arch-2 late in training, while GPQA, MATH, and MuSR also showed noisy results.

relationships.reason: The authors report MMLU-var ranks models by size throughout training (R2). The evidence is qualitative and figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: The authors reported that MMLU-var ranked models by size throughout the tested training trajectory.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
